Neonatal Thorny devils emerge from their leathery-shelled eggs after an incubation period that has been experimentally determined under controlled thermal conditions. Eggs maintained at a constant temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C] require approximately 105 days [ab = approximately 105 days] to complete embryonic development, a duration that reflects the relatively slow metabolic pace characteristic of this arid-zone agamid. At hatching, the young measure roughly 3.6 cm [Lb = roughly 3.6 cm] in snout–vent length, a diminutive size that immediately necessitates independent foraging for small ants, their primary prey. This age at birth, equivalent to about 15 weeks, is typical among reptiles that produce small clutch sizes and invest heavily in individual egg yolk reserves. The incubation temperature of 27 °C corresponds closely to the mean thermal conditions recorded in shallow subterranean nests in the species' arid Australian habitat, where diurnal fluctuations are buffered by the insulating properties of sandy soils. Hatchlings emerge with a full complement of scales and spines and are capable of locomotion and feeding within hours of eclosion.

As the juvenile matures, its growth trajectory is shaped by the pronounced seasonality and unpredictable rainfall of its desert environment. Individuals typically attain an ultimate snout–vent length of approximately 11 cm [Li = approximately 11 cm], which corresponds to a total length of roughly 18.8 cm when the tail is included. This relatively modest body size is an adaptation to a thermoregulatory strategy that relies on rapid heat absorption and dissipation through the spiny integument, which may also serve in predator defense and water collection. The conversion from total length to snout–vent length is standard in herpetological studies, facilitating comparisons across agamid taxa. Field surveys indicate that adult body size is achieved after several years of growth, during which the lizard's diet shifts from smaller to larger ant species as gape size increases. Under favorable conditions, individuals may reach this asymptotic size quickly, but in drought years, growth may slow considerably or even cease until resources become available again.

Reproductive output in the Thorny devil is limited by both clutch size and the frequency of breeding events. Females produce a single clutch of eggs each year [F_R_i = single clutch of eggs each year], with each clutch containing between 6 and 7 eggs [N_R_i = each clutch containing between 6 and 7 eggs]. These values, recorded at an ambient temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C] typical of the spring and early summer active season, are consistent with the low reproductive rate expected for a long-lived lizard inhabiting a resource-poor environment. The leathery-shelled eggs are deposited in a burrow excavated by the female, which then covers them with sand before abandoning the nest. There is no parental care beyond oviposition. The total annual reproductive output is thus modest, a life-history pattern that is compensated for by relatively high adult survival rates and a long reproductive lifespan. This single-clutch strategy contrasts with the multiple-brood patterns seen in many temperate-zone lizards but is common among Australian arid-zone agamids.

The lifespan of Moloch horridus is remarkably extended for a lizard of its size, a trait linked to its low metabolic rate and effective anti-predator defenses. Field studies and captive records indicate that individuals can live for as long as 20 years [am = 20 years] when maintained at an average active-season temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This considerable longevity is associated with a slow pace of life, including late maturation, low fecundity, and high annual survival of adults. The spiny body armor and cryptic coloration provide substantial protection from avian and mammalian predators, while the ability to absorb moisture through the skin allows the lizard to hydrate passively from dew and rain. Long-term mark-recapture studies in Western Australia have documented individuals surviving across multiple decades, with some of the oldest known specimens exceeding 20 years. Such extended lifespans are more typical of chelonians or large-bodied squamates but are unusual among agamids of comparable mass.

Sexual maturation in the Thorny devil occurs relatively late in life, a pattern consistent with its slow growth and extended lifespan. Data from both captive colonies and wild populations indicate that the time since birth at puberty is approximately 3 years [tp = approximately 3 years], a duration measured under thermal conditions averaging 25 °C [T = 25 °C] during active periods. This three-year period reflects the time required for juveniles to reach the body size necessary for successful reproduction, including the attainment of the minimum adult snout–vent length. Males and females appear to mature at similar ages, though some studies suggest slight asynchrony, with males possibly maturing earlier. The delayed onset of reproductive activity is mirrored in the late age at first reproduction, which typically occurs in the following breeding season after maturity is attained. This life-history schedule, combining late maturation, low annual fecundity, and a long adult lifespan, positions Moloch horridus as an extreme example of a slow-paced, bet-hedging reproductive strategy among agamid lizards.
